en: Salutations to the illustrious Lord of the Ganas; having prostrated before the glorious Gaṇeśa and the gods, [this work is composed] by the great grace of the illustrious Sūryanārāyaṇa.
I shall state the definition of the accent (*svara*) regarding the action (*kriyā*), as [taught by] Bhaṭṭa, the son of Homa-kanyā-purasū:

"From that, the word *catvāri* and *param* [are used], and when [the verb] *aharat* has the acute accent on its first syllable (*ādyudāttavān*). Regarding this: the two words *tasmāt* and *catvāri*, being subsequent (*param*), [govern the rule]; in the expression *aharat*, the word for the action (*kriyā-śabdaḥ*)—namely *āharat*—becomes acutely accented on its first syllable (*ādyudātta*). For example: *somamāharattasmādyajñamukham* ("He brought the Soma; therefore it is the mouth of the sacrifice") and *sāsomañcāharaccatvāri ca* ("She brought both the Soma and the four"). Why is it said "when subsequent" (*evam param*)? [Consider: *somamāharattasminnindraḥ* ("He brought the Soma; in that [place] Indra [was]"). [And: *yajñamāharadyattadvittaṃ vedyam* ("He brought the sacrifice; that which is to be known is wealth").

*prāyacchat-trir-yavam-tasmāt-tasmai-tvā-eṣaḥ-evaṃ-paraḥ-prāyacchat-iti-atra-ayacchat-iti-padam-ādyudāttam-syāt-asīti-sakārānyavarṇe-pare-sati*. For example: *yat-triḥ-prāyacchat-triḥ*, *vasantāya-prāyacchad-yavam*, *jayān-prāyacchad-tasmāj-jayāḥ*, *prāyacchad-tasmād-aindrāvaiṣṇavam*. Why [is it said] "when followed by *asi*"? [Because otherwise]: *tat-prāyacchad-tasmāt-sahasradakṣiṇam*.

For he gave that to Indra; [the formula] "to him thee" [is used]. Why [is it said]? He gave the *ukthya* to him; [then] "to him thee" for the second time. He gave that to him; "this is thy womb. Why [is it said] "thus further"? He gave to Indra the Bull; the Fierce one gave that to him; he accepted that. [In the verses] regarding the battles.

When [the particle] *tam* (accusative singular) enters [the preceding word], it is like that which Soma produced; there too, the action would be as in the case of *dyu*. For example: *medhośvaṃ prāviśattamevāvarundhe* ("The sacrifice entered the horse; he wins that very [horse]"). Why "that" (*tam*)? [Consider: *tadyavaṃ prāviśattadyaveramata* ("That entered the barley; that rejoiced in the barley"). Why "in this way" (*evaṃ*)? [Consider: *sośvaṃ prāviśat sośvasya* ("He entered the horse; he [is] of the horse"). When [the particle] *āhṛtya* (having brought) precedes and [the particle] *prāha* (he spoke) follows, it is exactly like that. Why "like that" (*tādṛk*)? [Consider: *devamanuṣyebhyaḥ prāha na purā* ("He spoke to the gods and men, not before"). In these cases, it should be understood that the subsequent [word] is entirely low (anudātta). For example:
That which Soma produced and Agni consumed—what is that? Soma produced it and Agni consumed it.

They caused it to enter, they took it, they employed it, and by means of it, the ritual action was performed; here too [the particle *yat*] functions in this way. For example: "For they caused her to enter at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*); he bathes at a sacred ford. Why [is *tīrthe* used]? [To show: "They caused her to enter into the waters" (*tad apsu prāveśayan*). "They caused the initiation and austerity to enter into the waters. "That which the gods took as the kingdom by means of the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* [oblations], that belongs to the *rāṣṭrabhṛts*. Why [is *tat* used]? [To show: "The gods took the kingdom" (*rāṣṭram ādadata yad devāḥ*). "They employed the meters; by means of them, they attained success."

*Min* (shame) was [the wife], *māyā* (illusion) was [the priest]; *kumbhī* (pot) preceded *ādāt* (he took). Here too, there is a ritual action (*kriyā*). For example: "Whatever shame (*mindā*) was mine, Agni [was that]. Why [is it] *mindā*? [In the case of: "That indeed became my father; I am the sacrifice (*yajña*), for he was the *ukthya*. Why [is it] *māyā*? [In the case of: "He was the overlord (*adhipati*); together with the *kumbhī* he took [it]. [The word] *āśīḥ* (blessing) is [to be supplied]. Why [is it] *kumbhī*? [In the case of: "Whatever belongs to him, that [is it]. It is included because of its high pitch (*uccatva*) in the *saṃhitā*. [The phrase] "whatever belongs to them" is [to be supplied]. Why [is it] *syava*? [In the case of: "And thus there is no end to this very thing."

*bha* [is used] when preceded by *āśayat* and *adhi*, and *paribhūḥ* [is used] with *asi* and *sādi*. (4) Both indeed [are used] with *ajāmi*. Why [is it said] "with *ajāmi*"? Because of association (*sāhacaryāt*). Because of that association, [it is said] "with *ajāmi*. [The mantra: "With the mind he deposited the embryo" (*manasā garbha āśayat*). For by means of form one approaches their form, namely by means of gold. For by means of gold one approaches their form. What is the purpose of [specifying] "preceded by" (*hi pūrva*)? [In the example: "This gift of yours, O Agni, comes" (*etatte agne rādha aiti*). "You are encompassing on all sides" (*viśvataḥ paribhūrasi*). Why [specify] "*asi*"? Because at the time of *saṃhitā* there is no doubt regarding an initial acute accent (*ādyudātta*), the mention here is of "*asi*" [to exclude others]. Because it occurs at the end of a half-verse (*ardhānta*), it is due to this association (*sāhacaryāt*).

Regarding the two [mantras] "O slayer of Vṛtra, you are the slayer of Vṛtra" and "You are made by the self-power (svadhā)," one should understand that because there is an absence of the udātta accent at the time of the *padapāṭha*, this indicates that [the word] does not end in the middle of a hemistich (*ardharcānta*). By this method, the verbal action (*kriyāpada*) extends from [the beginning] up to "he brought the interrupted udātta of the *saṃhitā*" and so forth; it is stated that at the time of the *padapāṭha*, it becomes udātta on the first syllable. In the section "Indra for Vṛtra," regarding the words "slay" (*jahi*), "Indra," "hear these" (*śṛṇutemān*), "end" (*antaḥ*), "collects" (*cinute*), "drank" (*apāt*), "self-head" (*ātmaśīrṣa*), and "Indra," the meaning is that the verbal word "slay" (*jahi*) and "end" (*antaḥ*) should be udātta on the final syllable.

He hears; he piles. In this case, these two [words] also [apply]. He said, "Kill him," [but] "Do not kill mine. Therefore, one partakes following Viṣṇu. What is the purpose of this section? [It is to show: "Kill with this"—he approached with that. Here, there is a total low accent (*sarvānudātta*). "Hear this my call. Why "this" (*imam*)? Because he indeed said, "Hear! "Whoever piles the fire-altar without a body, he becomes bodiless. Whoever piles the fire-altar without a head, he becomes headless. Why "thus" (*evam*)? "For him he piles it for Yama," [meaning] "for destruction. In these cases, at the time of the *pada* recitation, there is a total low accent.

Regarding *prokṣitaṃ vīkṣitāya*: here, by the word "etc. (*ādi*), the two [prefixes] *pra* and *vi* are intended as having the acute accent (*udātta*). These two are *avagrahas* (separated in the *padapāṭha*). Even at the time of the *padapāṭha*, they remain acute-accented. Examples: *na prokṣito yat* ("not sprinkled, that which... *prokṣitaṃ gopāyata* ("protect what has been sprinkled") In *prokṣitam*, *pra* is [acute]; [then] *ukṣitam*; [then] *gopāyata*. Why [mention] the vowel *i*? [To exclude cases like: *ājyaṃ prokṣaṇam* ("clarified butter for sprinkling"). In *vīkṣitāya*, *vi* is [acute]; [then] *īkṣitāya*; [then] *svāhā*. Why [mention] *īkṣita*? [To exclude cases like: *vīkṣamāṇāya svāhā* ("to him looking on, svāhā"). [In the passage: *tato vai so vindata prajām* ("from that indeed he obtained offspring"), etc., the prefixes (*upasargas*) of these words are also high-pitched (*ucca*) even at the time of the *padapāṭha*. In some cases they are high-pitched; in some cases they are low-pitched (*nīca*).

Thus, because there is an absence of such a distinction (*vikalpa*), there would be no grasping of this [rule]. Furthermore, [the rule] "one should pile the fire-altar (*agniṃ cinute*) with everything low, when it follows the word *yat*"—as in: "When you pile the fire-altar with the *ūṣāḥ* for nourishment and procreation..."—there is the attainment of the acute accent (*udātta*) because it precedes the word *yat*. Moreover, because the non-acute (*anudātta*) is observed due to the rules of euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*) in "cinutetho. Here, at the time of the *padapāṭha*, the statement "everything is low" is initiated for the word *cinute*.
The remaining accent should also be understood by the wise through the combined (saṃhita) tone, as follows:

in cases such as *jaradaṣṭiḥ*, *yathāsát*, and *agrepaśyat*, because they are combinations of udātta accents, the resulting accent is indeed udātta. In cases such as *sóbhavat*, *sóbravīt*, *tébruvan*, and *tésmin*, there is a svarita combination. One should know that at the time of the *padapāṭha* (word-text), these are anudātta. [Examples include: *yānté gacchan ya eváṃ vidvān*; *tásya té dadatu yéṣāṃ prāṇósi svāhā*;
*yadyāvacchab-dakau*; *yátra yathādyúccaḥ*; *yató yádi*.

When the words *yat*, *yaccha*, *yatra*, *yadā*, *yathā*, *yarhi*, *yadi*, *yataḥ*, *hi*, and *ādyaudātta* (a word having the acute accent on its first syllable) precede, then up to the twelfth [word], that is, extending through twelve words, the first syllable becomes acute (*ādyudātta*). This applies to a verb (*kriyāśabda*) which then becomes accented. The first verb is "high" (*uccavān*); some have the acute accent on the first syllable, while others have the acute accent on the middle syllable.

The meaning is that something may have the acute accent (*udātta*) on the final syllable. For example: *yo vai devebhyaḥ pratiprocya yajñena yajate* (he who, having announced [the sacrifice] to the gods, performs the sacrifice with the sacrificial rite); *ya evaṃ vidvān rohiṇīṃ lakṣmaṇāṃ paṣṭhauhīṃ vārtraghnīṃ dadāti* (he who, knowing thus, gives a reddish-brown, marked, six-year-old cow that slays enemies)—in these cases, the acute accent is on the initial syllable (*ādyudātta*). In *yaścīyate yatsañcite* (whoever is piled up, when it has been piled), the acute accent is on the middle syllable (*madhyodātta*). In *yo vai yamaṃ devayajanam asyā aniryācyāgniṃ cinute* (he who, without having asked Yama for this earth as a place of sacrifice, piles the fire-altar), the acute accent is on the final syllable of *cinute* (*antodātta*). And: *ya evaṃ vidvāṃsa etā āsate*.

Those who undergo initiation on the Ekāṣṭakā day; [the sacrifice] which he employs—such is the summary. Those cups (grahas) which one should draw prior to the Āgrayaṇa: "By which, O Agni, thou carriest a thousand," "with which [they utter] speech," "to whom they speak behind his back," "for whom the honey flows forth," "from whichever womb"—Prajāpati created offspring. [The word] *ādya* is udātta-accented. Or, for him whose [offering] is not according to the deity: "May they give to thee, those of whom thou art the breath, svāhā! May they two give, of whom thou art the breath, svāhā!"

"In whatever season a man dies"—these are examples of the masculine gender for the word *yat*. Now, examples of the feminine gender are to be cited: "That body of mine which was in you"; "Whatever deities are in the assembly"; "With those [fingers] with which you give"; "That oblation which this *niṣṭakā* [stick] is"; "By the power of which [quarter] of the front half"; "From whichever [deities] he causes him to move away"; "Of whichever deity it is sacrificed"; "Those who were born from her"; "In whichever direction you are magnified."

Now, regarding the designation of the neuter gender: "When it belongs to Agni"; "When by this [the gods] [overcame] the Asuras"; "Whatever he does not secure through the sacrifice"; "That he anoints with curds mixed with honey"; "That he causes it to settle with this"—in these instances, within a compound, there is a verbal noun (*kriyāśabda*) that possesses the acute accent (*udātta*). Examples include: "Those very beings that [exist]"; "As much as the *agnihotra* was"; "As much as his seat was"; "As many cattle as [there were]"; and so forth. Also: "Wherever death arises"; "When for you, O mortal..."

Indeed, [this applies] to the sacrifice: "yataḥ" and "ucca"—what [is the purpose of these]? As in: *yataḥ puroḍāśaḥ kūrmo bhūtvānu prāsarpat* ("from where the sacrificial cake, having become a tortoise, crept after"); *yarhi paśum* ("when the animal"); *yathā nāgatāyātithyam* ("as hospitality for one who has not arrived"); *āsīdyadi vā tāvat* ("it was, or perhaps so much"); *hi rājanyo yajate* ("for the Rājanya sacrifices"); *siṃhīrhyeṣā rūpaṃ kṛtvā* ("for she, having assumed the form of a lioness"); *hyeṣa sanmanuṣyānupaiti* ("for being such, he approaches men"). "What about *prathamāgni*? As in: *yathā vai putraḥ* ("just as indeed a son"); *yadete gṛhyante* ("since these are taken"); *yā prajāḥ* ("those offspring"); *parābahurvai* ("indeed, many beyond"); *yo vai de prāṇa uttaraḥ* ("that which is indeed the higher vital breath").

He who thus pressed the Soma, who offered it with effort, [overcame] the cold; he who was for Mitra and Varuṇa, who was indeed that [sacrifice], according to the axle, and he who was the fire-priest—knowing this as it was upon the chariot, he became threefold through the re-piling of the altar.

Some maintain that the words *soma* and *agni* [are also such]. In this regard, there would be two pairs of action-words (*kriyāśabda*) mentioned in a single [context], as follows: "The offspring who depart" (*yāḥ prajāḥ parā bhavantīḥ*); "Become many indeed" (*bahurvai bhavataḥ*); "He who [worships] the gods" (*yo vai devān*); "That which with the upāṃśu-vessel and first" (*yadupāṃśupātreṇa prathamaśca*); "He who, knowing thus, stands near Agni" (*ya evaṃ vidvānagnimupatiṣṭhatehaḥ*); "That which Soma generated, Agni" (*yatsomaḥ prājanayadagniḥ*); "That which three times he offered, three times" (*yattriḥ prāyacchattriḥ*); "For what one meditates upon with the mind, that" (*yaddhi manasā dhyāyati tat*); "That which he mixes with milk for Maitrāvaruṇa" (*yanmaitrāvaruṇaṃ payasā śrīṇāti*).

He who, indeed, having failed to establish the Soma, runs about as if he has fallen into a pit—yet he who, knowing this, sacrifices with the Agniṣṭoma, when they carry him [the fire] forth, is then established like a yoked horse on a wagon. When he piles the *punar-citi* (re-piling), it is for the sake of the oblations; for life is one thing, and the Soma belonging to Varuṇa is another. It is just as when other cups are drawn for those who share the half-portion (*ardhin*); they bring the Soma. When that Soma is being brought here, he establishes the Soma right there. What is meant by "here"? He thus establishes that very Soma while bringing the Soma. As for what is given to them...

One should not perform [the rite] with the verse "For the earth, thee" even in the Soma sacrifice, nor with the preceding one (pūrvayā) when carrying the ladles in the Soma sacrifice. What is the point here? In the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), one approaches the Soma; thus he obtains it through the preceding one; thus he finds it through the preceding one. Why does it say "one should not perform"? Because if one were to perform it with the preceding one, one would make it futile (*chambaṭ*). And one places the calf over [the fire] at the end of the night, before sunrise.
For example: "He releases the calf and does not cause it to go near the fire. What [is the result]? He places [the pot] on the fire and strikes [the grain].
[The word] *apa* is repeated from the beginning up to the end of *yuṣmad*. Example: *apa yuṣmad akramīt*. Why is it said "from the beginning, when there is no vowel"? Example: *vi hvayāmahai*.
And Agni, not being hungry, formerly drank the Soma with his mouth;
Agni [is] among those gods in that [place], and there are three accounts regarding the cow.
Soma is indeed Agni for him, through the upright and by means of what is boneless and true.
"The Ādityas and all the Viśvedevas stood by that imperishable milk in yonder world.

(13) Thus, the preceding [section] up to the fifth word shall have its verb raised in pitch (*udātta*). For example: *nakṣodhuko bhavati*, *nāsya rudraḥ*, *sā somaṃ cāharaccatvāri cākṣarāṇi*, *adhvāno'bhūvan*, *agniḥ puraḥ bhavati*, *ava sabhāṃ rundhe*, *agniramum̐lloka āsīt*, *agnirdevānāṃ dūta āsīt*, *trīṇi ca śatānyasṛjyanta*, *somaśca*, *kathā somāyātithyaṃ kriyate*, *tattveḍā gavyairayat*. What about *ā*? (Note: The text provided contains a mix of Vedic citations and grammatical rules regarding accentuation (*svarita*). The translation focuses on rendering the cited examples and the rule.)

Soma alone bestows seed upon him; Agni alone brings forth progeny for him. What then is the meaning of "tatparā" (that beyond)? Soma indeed found a thousand; Agni departed from the gods. For what reason? Because of the truth, [progeny is produced] by means of that which is boneless; for what reason? Because of the truth, the cups for two deities are drawn from a single vessel. What then is the meaning of "evaṃpara" (thus beyond)? For what reason? Because of the truth, on both sides by means of the Gāyatrī; the Ādityas prospered in yonder world by means of two three-day periods, and in this world by means of the *caru* offering. For what reason? Because of the truth, the Ādityas prospered in yonder world; [the gods prospered] in this world by means of the *caru*. What then is the meaning of "ādityā" (the Ādityas)?

In that world, he prospers through the *caru* offering; on the full moon day, he becomes *acyuta* (unshakable). His vow is to subsist on milk. "O Viśvedevas, hear this my invocation! Stand by me! Strike!"—thus [he says].
Or else, from another source, during the bright fortnight, one should likewise [recite] up to the fifth [verse] among the preceding ones.

The word *vā* and the word *anya*, when occurring first, should have the acute accent (*udātta*) up to the fifth occurrence of a verb (*kriyā-śabda*) within a *pūrvapakṣa*. For example: *yajño vā vai yajñapatim duhe*; *anye vā vai nidhim aguptaṃ vindanti*; *sa vā anyaṃ jinīyāt*; *antarvedy anyaḥ pādo bhavati*; *anyo naḍvān bhavati*; *anyā yanti*. Why "in a *pūrvapakṣa*" (*pūrvapakṣe*)? [Counter-examples: *agnicit vā agniṃ duhe tām*; *savyena yajño vasvī ca*; *dvir ninānāyatanān ṛṇam*;
*yavaṃ saudāsā nabho rdhvo rathacakram parāsu ca*.

Thus, when another [word] is drawn forward (ākṛṣṭa), the preceding verbal form shall take the high accent up to the fifth [word]. For example: "The right one is yoked; the left one is not. "Neither does the Adhvaryu become blind, nor the sacrifice. "'And you are wide, and you are wealthy,' he says. "He offers twice. "He wipes twice. "He does not die prematurely. "He is not without a dwelling place. "He becomes free from debt to the ancestors. "That is his freedom from debt to the deity. "He gave barley to Spring. "From that indeed he obtained offspring; he prevailed over the Saudāsas."

One should pile the fire-altar in the form of a chariot wheel (*rathacakracita*) to drive away one's rivals and those yet to be born. Why [is it] "in this manner" (*evam*)? [Because] "one drives away one's rivals by offering oblations while stepping forward" (*abhikrāmam juhoti*); "thereby the gods prospered and the Asuras were defeated. And [the term] *saṃbaddha* (connected) refers to proximity; between two equal [terms], the one with the higher vowel is [placed first]. 15.

When there is a previously established attainment indicated by the letter *ca*, a verb connected with that action is pronounced with a high pitch (*uccaiḥ*). For example: "In the world, they prosper by means of two three-day periods"; "I shall drive away my rivals who have been born. Even when two similar words are in proximity, the second one is pronounced with a high pitch. For example: "He crosses, he crosses"; "He saw, he saw. If they are not in proximity, the first word containing the sound *sa* is pronounced with a high pitch. For example: "He exists by himself; he is excluded from this"; "That which belonged to the Asuras was [destroyed]. [Thus] he elevates himself by means of the Brahman. Why is it said "the first"? [Consider: "He suppresses his rival."

In "mayati," "vaṣaṭ," "stṛṇute," "tṛtīya," and "rundhe," as well as in "yunakti," "prajāpate," "asya," "pāhi," and so forth, and at the beginning of a *yajus*, there should be two syllables with the *udātta* accent. For example: [text omitted].

He causes [the horse] to go by means of the *yājyā* verse; by the *vaṣaṭ*-call, he strikes it down with the second [verse], and with the third. He secures the remnants; he conquers the world of heaven. Thus he yokes it; he unyokes it by means of Prajāpati. "Thou art to be praised and to be lauded, O steed; thou art Yama, thou art Āditya, O courser; thou art Agni, rich in light. "May Mitra be gracious, may the Son of the Waters be gracious. "Protect the sacrifice, protect the lord of the sacrifice; protect me today from heaven; protect me, O Agni!"—thus they say three times.

Thus, in words such as *asi* and *śabda*, the entire aggregate [of syllables] becomes udātta starting from the *yajus* portion; this has been stated. What is the purpose of specifying "starting from the *yajus*"? [Examples follow: *vasvy asi*; *viṣṇoḥ kramo 'si*; *tad astu tubhyam*; *tayā naḥ pāhi*; *prāṇaṃ me pāhi*; *trīṇi ta āhur divi*.
[The rule applies to] *naghnīṇi*, *ṛṣabham*, *dvedhā*, *dvedhāḥ*, *kriyā*, and others that do not participate in other [specific] recited portions (*śruti*).

In this way, the preceding action would not be accompanied by the *uccaiḥ* (loud) intonation. For example: "If the *vārtraghnī* [verse] were recited with the ear-grasping [intonation]. Examples: "If the *anustaraṇī* cow were tied to the foot [of the sacrificer], the sacrificer would die prematurely. "If he places a bull upon each layer of bricks as they are being piled. "If he collects all human [implements] together, two by two. The word *iṅgyabhāgnya* would not be the cause [for the modification]. Another *sāman* occurs. Just as Manu and humans, and as those who live by sacrifice, so [it is]. 17.

These signs would not exist. As Manu is among men, so it is [with others]. As indeed are men: "He who performs the New and Full Moon sacrifices, morning and evening"—what is meant by this? It means he who, being a performer of the New and Full Moon sacrifices, does not fall away from the deities according to their respective portions.

The head and so forth, the *dhruva* vessel, the saline soil (*ūṣāḥ*), the two downward-flowing [streams], the clarified butter (*ājya*), and the loose earth (*purīṣa*); the embers, the reddish-brown bamboo, the goat, the altar (*vedi*), and whatever else follows. 18.

In this way, the word *yat* [in the subsequent rule] would be redundant. For example: *yacchīrṣṇāśīr*, *ṣaktimānthsyāt*, *yaddhruva uttamo grahāṇāṃ gṛhyate*. Why say "at the beginning"? [Counter-examples: *yaddhruva ātmā hotā*, *yadūṣāḥ puṣṭyāmeva*, *yadanvañcau puroḍāśau*, *yadājyamapyeva naḥ*, *yatpurīṣamagnimeva*, *yadaṅgāreṣu bhaviṣyat*, *yadvāruṇassākṣāt*, *yadveṇossuṣiram*, *yadajā vaśā vāyavyām*, *yadvedirmedhyām*, *upahyātmano devānāṃ suvargāśvācca cakṣuṣī*.
For Rudra places the earthen [head] alone below. In this way, the particle *hi* would otherwise be redundant. For example:

"The self (*ātman*) indeed [is the portion] of those invited"; "Offspring (*prajā*) indeed [is] more intimate than the self"; "These indeed [are] the portions of the gods"; "Heavenly world (*suvarga loka*) indeed [is] as if above"; "A donkey indeed [is] inferior to a horse"; "Two eyes indeed [are] equal"; "Rudra indeed [comes] from the northern half once as it were"; "The Audumbara [wood] indeed [is] not fit for an oblation because it is earthen. Why [is it said] "the low tone is *anudātta*"? [To exclude cases where it is not so].
As he previously conquers, so far as he pours out the grain; in these [bricks] he places the Soma. What is meant by "exclusively"? As he lays down the *stomabhāga* bricks:
among those to be piled (*cityā*), some are different and others are not; some are in front and others are otherwise.
Of that [set], he should lay down the different ones among those to be piled; he should not lay down any other subsequent brick; he should not offer any other oblation in front.
He places other bricks facing westward in front. If it were otherwise, [the sequence would be] from both sides. Why not? Because both [ways] are indeed non-repetitive (*ajāmi*).

Having grasped the *ghāryā* bricks, that which is placed in the middle—when the word "that" (*tat*) stands in the *anīcakā* position, and even when the numeral word ends in *-na*, there is proximity; it is not a single group of eight.

If there is a pause between a noun and a verb, or between two words, then [the following] would not be raised in pitch (*udātta*). For example: *yad āghāra ātmā paśur āghāram āghārya* (when the self is the libation, having poured the libation); *yac citrāpūrṇamāso mukhataḥ* (that which is the Citrā and the Full Moon at the beginning). Why is it said "after *ā*"? [Consider: *yo vai śraddhām anārabhya yajñena yajate* (he who indeed sacrifices with a sacrifice without having undertaken faith). In this case, the *vyāhṛtis* are raised in pitch. For example: *yad antarikṣaṃ tad u me pitābhūt* (what was the intermediate space, that became my father); *yat saumyo brahmavarcasaṃ tena* (what was the Soma, by that [he obtains] spiritual luster); *yad dvādaśakapālas tena vaiśvānarāt* (what was the cake on twelve potsherds, by that from Vaiśvānara); *yā veve devānāṃ harītābhyām* (what was the separation of the gods, by the two yellow ones).

As for those which are barren, or both [barren and non-barren]: those which are the first [are for] the sacrifice; on the fourth day, that which is twelve-spoked; on the twelfth day, that which is nine-potherded—by means of the *trivṛt* (ninefold) hymn, he places [the sacrifice] within him. "In the enclosure" (*vāre vṛte*)—for the third part of this [sacrifice] has been enclosed by the slaying of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*). Why "not low-lying" (*anīcaka*)? He makes her the last among the *anustaraṇī* cows. For those who, knowing thus, sacrifice with the four-night rite (*catūrātra*), and those who, knowing thus, sit for the thirty-three-day session (*trayastriṃśadaham*). Why "without a crack" (*anedanta*)?

That which [is performed] with the *abhijit* sacrifice in the third year; that on the fourth day the *āgrayaṇa* cup is drawn; that there are two ropes on a single sacrificial post (*yūpa*). What is excluded by the term "not one" (*aneka*)? One makes a bull one-year-old (*ekahāyana*); "he buys Soma with a tawny one-year-old cow. The word "first" (*prathama*) refers to a single thing, excluding its occurrence as a synonym for the pronoun *tat*. For example: "or he who is the first animal over the piled fire. Why is it not eightfold (*nāṣṭaka*)? As in: "that which belongs to Agni, consisting of eight potsherds, occurs on the new moon day."

What is meant by "absence" (asānnidhya)? [It refers to cases such as: "Those Keśins who first sat for the sacrificial session"; "When the second Hotṛ is the Apratiratha"; "The meter when there is a cake on twelve potsherds"; and "By whose power [there is power] for both. But surely, in the case of "to the Aśvins, to Pūṣan," how can there be high pitch even from a distance? We reply: because it consists of a single *yajus*. Furthermore, even in what is not a *pūrva-yajus*, the action is always [performed]; this is established as another type of *yajus*. 21.

For example: "Whatever [gift] he should bestow upon the ancestors"; why say "always"? [Because it occurs in: "The Agnihotra of one who knows thus"; "We choose him as our messenger," he recites; "That which is the lotus-leaf, by its very form [he wins] it"; "That which belongs to the Adābhya when it is bound"; "That which is the Traidhātavīya"; "He for whom there are verses containing the word *pratiṣṭhā* [sacrifices] behind; he indeed stands firm behind"; "For he sacrifices eleven after-sacrifices (*anūyāja*) created behind"; "For Vaiśvānara is life by way of deity."

For the Rājanya is of the *triṣṭubh* metre, and the ashes are in the waters; he thus yokes Agni in his full extent. Because the *marutvatīya* cups are [offered] with the first [verse], and because it is said, "he strews with whichever [verse]";
for he is not that, for they are those, for she is her, for that is his illusion, for it is so.
May those which go to her go; that which is in her, that which is theirs, and indeed here. 22.

In the cases of *yo yakṣye*, *yasyaivaṃ yattaṃ*, *yāvāneva yaṅ*, and *yaṅ* as well—since the prohibition of the high-pitched (*udātta*) accent applies here due to the intervention of the word *tat* and others, this particle *na* serves as a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*). For example: *trirhi sa taṃ tasmai prāyacchat*; *tīrthe hi te tāṃ prāveśayan*; *yajño hi tasya māyāsīt*. Why [is it] *māyā*? [As in: *vāyurhi tasya pavayitā*; *hi tadveda*. *Yānte gacchan ya evam*; *yastasyāndiśi*; *yattadvittaṃ vedyam*; *yeṣāṃ hyeṣa bhāgaḥ*; *yo yakṣya ityuktvā*.

"For one who knows thus, the *udābhyas* are drawn; that which he has not accomplished through sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇās*), as much as the sacrifice itself, that he recovers at the end. This is because [the passage] does not fall within the scope of a single *yajus* formula beginning with "those who shall increase the lord of the sacrifice" (*ye yajñapatiṃ vardhāni*).
Indeed, it was described as being "for the sake of children" (*bālānām*) in order to indicate its specific accentuation.
Thus ends the complete commentary.
